description: Where a secret comes from. One resolution order, applied by both implementations to every value in `secrets` below, so that a deployment configures a password once and reaches the same database, relay or key from either path.
principle: A secret in an environment variable is readable in /proc/<pid>/environ, is inherited by every child process, and turns up in `docker inspect`, in crash dumps and in CI logs. So the environment may carry a *path* to a secret, and the best of the three sources carries no environment entry at all. The variable itself stays supported, because a development machine has no reason to build a file for a password nobody is hiding.

resolution.description: The first source that has the secret wins. Every one of them is looked at in this order, for each name in `secrets`.

sources.name: systemd credential
sources.description: `LoadCredential=`, `ImportCredential=` or `SetCredential=` in the unit file. systemd places the secret as a file in a per-unit directory on a tmpfs, readable by the service user alone, and names that directory in $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY. Nothing here is a systemd API: an implementation reads a file at a path it was told, which is why both paths can use it and why no library is needed.
sources.credentialName: Exactly the name of the variable, so that `ls $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY` and the unit file and this table all say the same word. `LoadCredential=DB_PASSWORD:/etc/gradido/db_password`.
sources.note: Skipped where $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY is unset, which is every platform that is not a systemd service. Nothing about the other two sources changes there.

sources.name: file named by the environment
sources.description: The variable holds a path and the secret is the file's content. This is the convention the official postgres and mysql container images use, and it is how docker and kubernetes secrets arrive: as files that are mounted, not as environment entries.

sources.name: the environment
sources.description: The value itself. Lowest of the three because it is the one that leaks.

rules.name: A named source that cannot be read is fatal
rules.statement: When <NAME>_FILE is set and the file cannot be read, the process refuses to start. It does not fall back to <NAME>. The same holds for a credential file that exists and cannot be read.
rules.why: A silent fallback turns an unreadable secret into an empty one, and an empty password is how a process connects as somebody else or fails much later with a message about the wrong thing. Configuration that names a source is a promise that the source is there.

rules.name: One trailing line ending is removed and nothing else
rules.statement: A single trailing "\n" or "\r\n" is stripped from a file's content. Nothing else is trimmed: no leading whitespace, no other trailing whitespace, no quotes.
rules.why: `echo secret > file` writes a newline that is not part of the secret, and systemd copies a file verbatim. Trimming further would make a password that legitimately ends in a space impossible to configure, and a secret nobody can express is worse than one that needs a careful `printf`.

rules.name: An empty result is a value, not an absence
rules.statement: A source that is present and yields an empty string has answered. Resolution stops there and the secret is the empty string.
rules.why: Otherwise an operator who deliberately configures no password gets the next source instead, which is the surprise this whole order exists to avoid.

rules.name: A tool that writes configuration down must ask where a secret came from
rules.statement: Anything that offers a secret's current value and writes the answer back -- `setup`, which edits the `.env` -- skips a secret whose source is the credential or the file, and says so instead of asking.
rules.why: Otherwise the mechanism is undone by pressing Enter: the value resolved out of a tmpfs systemd guards, or out of a file with permissions of its own, would be written into a file in the working directory. A protection that a prompt can downgrade is not one. Only the environment source may be rewritten, because rewriting it is what `setup` is for.

secrets.name: DB_PASSWORD
secrets.description: The PostgreSQL password. Empty is correct over a Unix socket under peer authentication -- see database-config.json, rules.password, which is a separate question from where the value comes from.

secrets.name: EMAIL_PASSWORD
secrets.description: The SMTP password. Empty is correct for a relay that wants no credentials -- a MailDev in a compose stack -- and it is empty together with EMAIL_USERNAME or not at all: SMTP AUTH is a pair, and half of one is a session that authenticates as nobody.

notes: The list above is short because the services are. A secret added to either implementation is added here first: an operator who learns DB_PASSWORD_FILE has learned the mechanism, and a second secret that resolved differently would make that knowledge wrong. The JWT signing key is the next one this file is waiting for -- it has no environment variable yet, and when it gets one it gets a line here in the same breath.

A `.env` file is not one of the sources. It is read before any of this -- dotenv for the reference path, fast-servers/service-core/src/env_file.c for the C one, which also writes it for `setup` -- and it only fills variables that are unset, so what it provides is source 3 and never overrides a real environment entry. It is a convenience for a single-machine installation and not a way to deploy a secret.
